passages.¶1: I recently got introduced to this game called Can't Stop and it got me thinking about probabilities. In this post, I'll take you through probability foundations, column choice, when to stop, continuing vs switching, strategy head-to-heads, and designer balance.
passages.¶10: P(can make a 7) = 834/1296 approx 64.4% via inclusion-exclusion over A=(1,6), B=(2,5), C=(3,4): each 302/1296, pairwise overlaps 24/1296 each, triple overlap 0. Two-dice P(7) was 16.67%.
passages.¶11: Complete four-dice table: sums 2 to 12 run 171 (13.2%), 302 (23.3%), 461 (35.6%), 580 (44.8%), 727 (56.1%), 834 (64.4%) symmetric. Normalized probability ratio 2-to-7 is 4.88; length ratio is 4.33. Pretty close.
passages.¶12: Expected rolls = length/probability. Column 2: 3/0.132 = 22.73 rolls. Column 7: 13/0.644 = 20.18 rolls. Full table: 2/12 need 22.73, 3/11 need 21.46, 4/10 need 19.67, 5/9 need 20.09, 6/8 need 19.60, 7 needs 20.18.
passages.¶13: You have THREE active columns and bust if you can't hit ANY of them. Columns {6,7,8}: 1193/1296 = 92.0% success. Columns {2,3,12}: 568/1296 = 43.8% success, more likely to bust than succeed.
passages.¶14: All 165 three-column combinations ranked. Top: {6,7,8} 92.0% success, 8.0% bust, 39.8% clean, Q 1.43. Bottom: {2,11,12} 43.8% success, 56.2% bust, 2.3% clean, Q 1.05. 37 combos excellent (>=85%), median 79.6%.
passages.¶15: Keep rolling if (P_success x Q) > (P_bust x U). On {6,7,8} with 5 unsaved steps: expected loss 0.08x5=0.4; expected gain 0.92x1.43=1.32. Since 1.32 > 0.4, keep rolling.
passages.¶16: On {2,3,12} with 2 unsaved steps: risk 0.562x2=1.12; gain 0.438x1.05=0.46. Since 1.12 > 0.46, STOP. Clean moves only: 39.8% on {6,7,8}; 2.3% on {2,3,12}. Forced-move rule balances {6,7,8}.
passages.¶17: Should you continue current columns or switch? Mathematics favor continuation in most cases, but forced-move contamination sometimes forces switches. Author notes quantitative always-continue vs switch analysis is open future work.
passages.¶18: I tested 38 strategies across 14 strategic families: Baseline; Conservative(k) k in {1,2,3,4}; Heuristic(alpha) alpha in {0.3,0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}; OpponentAware four variants; Greedy-Improved; Adaptive; Proportional; Progressive; Probabilistic; Column-Count; Outside/Middle; Runner-Aware; Column-Quality; Hybrid/Advanced.
passages.¶19: Single-player (1,000 trials each): GreedyUntil1Col 10.5 turns median 9 std 5.73 busts 7.50; FiftyPercentSurvival 11.3 turns; top 15 span 10.5-12.8 turns. Conservative Heuristic(2.0) and MonteCarloLookahead average under 1 bust per game.
passages.¶2: The rules are straightforward: roll four dice, pair them up however you want, move your markers. You can keep rolling as long as you want, but if you can't move any of your three active markers, you lose everything gained that turn.
passages.¶20: Head-to-head: 38 strategies, 2,500 games per matchup, 3.6M total. FiftyPercentSurvival 69.84% (132,696/190,000); Heuristic(1.5) 66.46%; Heuristic(2.0) 63.26%. Overall first-player advantage +11.18% (P1 wins 55.59%). GreedyUntil1Col bias +31.24%.
passages.¶21: Champion FiftyPercentSurvival: roll until cumulative survival drops below 50%, n = log(0.5)/log(P_success). Column prefs: Column 8 (42.0%), Column 7 (38.4%), Column 6 (37.7%). Beats GreedyUntil1Col 55.22%, Heuristic(1.5) 54.38%; self-play 50.00%.
passages.¶22: Single-column deviations at most +/-13.6%. Perfect balance would need Column 2/12: 171 steps and Column 7: 834 steps, about an 8-hour game. Optimal +-1-step board [3,5,8,10,12,14,12,10,8,5,3] cuts deviation to +/-3.09%, 4x better with +1 step.
passages.¶23: Best balance under 20 steps: [4,7,11,14,17,20,17,14,11,7,4], +/-2.17%, 6x improvement. Best linear step=2.25 keeps [3,5,8,10,12,14,...] at +/-3.09%; integer step base=5 step=4 gives +/-3.32%. Multi-column reality: Column 7 in {6,7,8} finishes in ~2 turns vs Column 2 in {2,3,12} in ~30 turns.
passages.¶24: Conclusion: four-dice flattens distribution (P7 64.4% vs P2 13.2%, 4.88x vs 6x); combos matter ({6,7,8} 92% vs {2,3,12} 44%); probabilistic strategies dominate; consistency beats speed; P1 advantage 55.59%; forced-move rule compensates imbalance; perfect balance unnecessary.
passages.¶25: For players: use FiftyPercentSurvival, aim for columns 5-9, avoid columns 2-3 and 11-12, prioritize consistency. For designers: prioritize playability over perfection, consider handicaps. Open question: can any strategy break 75%, or is ~70% the limit?
passages.¶26: All code and data: probability_calculations.py; column_combinations.py; strategies_correct_implementation.py (38 strategies); comprehensive_benchmark_enhanced.py; 3.6M games in 3.89 hours; COMPREHENSIVE_RESULTS.md; column_combinations_all.csv; strategy_analysis_updated.md.
passages.¶3: The board has columns numbered 2 through 12, with lengths: 2 and 12: 3 steps; 3 and 11: 5; 4 and 10: 7; 5 and 9: 9; 6 and 8: 11; 7: 13. You need to complete three columns to win.
passages.¶4: I've implemented a fully interactive web version with Python/FastAPI backend and React frontend. You can play it online and check out the source code.
passages.¶5: Critical rule: you must take all available moves. If your chosen pairing creates any valid move, you must make ALL legal moves from that pairing, even unwanted ones. Example: on {6,7,8} rolling (1,1,3,4) as 2+7 forces taking BOTH 2 and 7.
passages.¶6: Two-dice baseline table: sums 2..12 have 1,2,3,4,5,6,5,4,3,2,1 ways out of 36 (2.78% to 16.67%). Sum 7 at 16.67% is exactly 6x more likely than sum 2 at 2.78%.
passages.¶7: Quick proof: P(sum 2) = 1/6 x 1/6 = 1/36; P(sum 7) has 6 ordered ways. If Can't Stop used two dice, column 7 would need to be 6x longer than column 2, but it is only 13/3 approx 4.3x longer.
passages.¶8: In Can't Stop you roll FOUR dice then pair them up. Example roll 2,3,4,5 gives (2,3)+(4,5)=5 and 9; (2,4)+(3,5)=6 and 8; (2,5)+(3,4)=7 and 7. Just three possible pairings.
passages.¶9: P(can make a 2) needs at least two 1s: P(zero 1s)=(5/6)^4=625/1296; P(exactly one 1)=500/1296. Therefore P = 1-625/1296-500/1296 = 171/1296 approx 13.2%, way higher than two-dice 2.78%.

meta.title: Can't Stop probability and strategy analysis

nodes.text: Can't Stop analysis: four dice flatten odds, middle columns dominate, consistent probabilistic strategies win, design favors playability.
Roll four dice, pair freely, advance three active markers; bust loses the turn's progress.
Columns 2-12 have lengths 3-5-7-9-11-13-11-9-7-5-3; complete three columns to win.
Forced-move rule: chosen pairing forces ALL its legal moves, even unwanted ones.
(1,1,3,4) as 2+7 on {6,7,8} forces taking both 2 and 7.
Two-dice baseline peaks at 7 with 16.67%, exactly 6x likelier than 2 at 2.78%.
Sums 2-12 have 1-2-3-4-5-6-5-4-3-2-1 ways of 36; 1 way versus 6 ordered ways.
Column 7 is only about 4.3x longer (13/3) than column 2, not 6x.
Four-dice pairing offers three pairings and sharply flattens the distribution.
P(can make 2) = 171/1296 approx 13.2%, up from two-dice 2.78%.
P(can make 7) = 834/1296 approx 64.4% via inclusion-exclusion; overlaps 24/1296, triple 0.
Full range 13.2% to 64.4%; probability ratio 4.88 nearly matches length ratio 4.33.
Three-column combination choice dominates single-column odds.
Expected rolls L/P: column 2 needs 22.73, column 7 needs 20.18 rolls.
{6,7,8} succeeds 1193/1296 = 92.0% with Q 1.43 markers per roll.
{2,3,12} succeeds only 568/1296 = 43.8% with Q 1.05; bust likelier.
All 165 combos ranked; 37 excellent at 85%+, median 79.6%, worst 43.8%.
Clean moves only: 39.8% for {6,7,8} and 2.3% for {2,3,12}.
Keep rolling while expected gain exceeds expected loss.
Rule: continue if (P_success x Q) > (P_bust x U); {6,7,8} gives 1.32 > 0.4.
{2,3,12} with 2 steps gives 1.12 > 0.46 loss, so stop.
Continuation usually beats switching, but full quantitative comparison remains open future work.
Tournament of 38 strategies across 14 families over 3.6M games crowns FiftyPercentSurvival.
Scale: 1,000 trials per strategy, 2,500 games per matchup, 3.6M games total.
Fastest GreedyUntil1Col 10.5 turns (median 9, sd 5.73, 7.50 busts); top 15 span 10.5-12.8.
Champion FiftyPercentSurvival 69.84% (132,696/190,000); Heuristic(1.5) 66.46% second.
Champion stops when cumulative survival drops below 50%: n = log(0.5)/log(P_success).
Paradox: GreedyUntil1Col #1 speed but #11 at 58.90%; consistency beats speed.
First-player advantage +11.18% overall (P1 wins 55.59%); GreedyUntil1Col bias +31.24%.
Opponent-aware tweaks did not help; web game plus full code and data released.
Board fits 1980 constraints; forced-move rule compensates residual imbalance.
Single-column deviations stay within +/-13.6% given integer lengths.
Perfect balance needs 171 vs 834 steps, about an 8-hour game.
Optimal +-1-step board [3,5,8,10,12,14,12,10,8,5,3] cuts deviation to +/-3.09%, 4x better.
Best under-20 board [4,7,11,14,17,20,17,14,11,7,4] hits +/-2.17%; integer linear design +/-3.32%.
Advice: play 50% rule on columns 5-9; designers prioritize playability plus handicaps.
